summary:
Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Montenegro since 1977, with an equal age of consent of 14, and no prohibition has been restored. A trans visitor faces no legal exposure for being trans or for presenting in a gender non-conforming way in public.

The Law on Prohibition of Discrimination, passed on 27 July 2010, lists gender identity as a prohibited ground and reaches employment, the provision of goods and services, education and health services. Criminal Code amendments adopted in 2013 and in force from 3 June 2014 prohibit hate speech based on gender identity and provide penalty enhancements where an offence is committed because of the victim's LGBT status, gender identity included.

Those enhancements are applied unevenly. The European Commission has found that prosecutors bring misdemeanour charges where hate-crime proceedings are warranted, which limits the sentence range and the deterrent effect.

Legal gender change remains restrictive: a person may change their legal gender only after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and sterilisation, obtaining a medical diagnosis, and divorcing if married. Montenegro had not, by November 2025, adopted the Draft Law on Legal Recognition of Gender Identity based on self-determination, missing its 2024 adoption deadline under the EU accession programme despite completed legislative steps and consultations; no fair, transparent, self-determination-based framework is in place.

Public hostility is documented. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) records continued anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric, with over 222 online hate-speech incidents reported. In that period a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on television was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks, with police response monitored. A study found only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation.

Organised hostility and state protection have both been visible at Pride events. The first Podgorica Pride, scheduled for May 2011, was cancelled after two attacks on gay people in the capital. The first Pride eventually marched in Podgorica in October 2013: roughly 150 marchers guarded by some 2,000 police, with rock-throwing opponents stopped by tear gas.

Relationship recognition is partial. The Constitution bans same-sex marriage. Parliament approved a Life Partnership law on 1 July 2020 by a 42-5 vote, signed 3 July 2020 and published 7 July 2020, in effect from 15 July 2021, granting almost the same rights as opposite-sex marriage except adoption. An earlier Draft Law on Same-Sex Partnership adopted by the Government in December 2018 would have granted near-marriage-equivalent rights via registrar ceremony while explicitly excluding parenting, foster care and adoption; MPs blocked a same-sex partnership law on 31 July 2019 despite government backing, leaving couples without hospital visitation or shared-benefit rights at that time.

A 2018 ERA study found 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins were closeted. Gays, lesbians and bisexuals are not banned from military service.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 notes a new Action Plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI Strategy was adopted with a budget of €45,000, alongside the continued hate-speech trend.

GlobalGayz (March 2012) describes a small gay scene existing alongside deeply entrenched anti-gay opinion, with discrimination and harassment when visible.

Human Dignity Trust records that Montenegro decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1977, placing it alongside Croatia and Slovenia as a European cohort of that year.

outOfScopeNotes:

The status of the Draft Law on Legal Recognition of Gender Identity after the missed 2024 deadline is unresolved in the inventory beyond its non-adoption as of November 2025.
